title: Policy bundle
description:
The body of `GET /v1/policy-bundle` — the ruleset an enforcement point caches and evaluates every request against.

What this schema can express is shape. Three of the bundle's rules are about meaning and are stated here in prose because no schema carries them:

1. **An endpoint with no binding entry is subject to every policy in `policies`.** An empty `bindings` list means nothing is narrowed, not that nothing applies. Read the other way round it is a total loss of enforcement.
2. **A failed fetch is not an empty bundle.** An empty chain allows, so a reader that treats an unreachable control plane as a bundle with no rules converts an outage of Rail Center into an outage of enforcement. Keep serving the last bundle held. A reader that has **never** held one is in a different state and forwards rather than refusing: it has been told no posture at all, so refusing enforces a decision the control plane never made — and it would black-hole traffic on a gateway whose posture is `none` or `observe`, which is the one thing those values exist to promise. What keeps traffic off a reader in that state is readiness: report unready until a bundle is held. Where nothing honours readiness the window is real, and this says so rather than closing it with a refusal that is wrong more often than it is right.
3. **A bundle valid against this schema can still be unusable.** Four classes: a policy id or a bound id in a spelling the contract does not name; a `schema_version` or a `content_hash` carrying a character no log line can hold; a duplicate policy id; and two bindings for one endpoint. Three of the four are beyond what this file can say. Uniqueness across a list has no keyword at all. Those two strings' character rule is defined by Unicode general category. `pattern` is ECMA-262, which can say that with `\p{...}` under the `u` flag — but a reader validating with Python's `jsonschema` cannot, because it compiles patterns with `re`, and enumerating the code points instead would be a snapshot that a later Unicode revision silently invalidates. A rule half the readers of this file cannot evaluate is worse than one stated in prose. The id grammar *is* expressible as a `pattern`, and is deliberately not written as one: it would be a second copy of a rule that already lives in code and in vectors, and the loop that produced this file kept finding second copies that had stopped agreeing with the first. The `gated`/`open` arity rules are the one case where a schema rule is both expressible and cheap to keep true, so they are stated below.

A reader is therefore not conformant by validating against this file. It is conformant by passing the vectors that accompany it.

schema_version.description: The shape of this document, so a reader can tell an unsupported bundle from a malformed one and refuse it whole rather than half-read it. At the root beside `content_hash` because it describes the document: a reader must find it before parsing, so it cannot live inside a sub-object whose own shape it explains. Named `schema_version` rather than `version` because a content hash sits beside it and only one of the two is a version.

content_hash.description: A content hash of the `schema_version`, the `enforcement`, the `binding_fallback`, the policies *and* the bindings. A reader re-fetching on a timer compares it and re-parses only when it changes. Bindings are covered because attaching a policy to an endpoint changes which requests are denied without changing any policy; `binding_fallback` is covered because it decides every unmatched call; `schema_version` is covered because a reader that must refuse an unsupported shape has to discover the bump. **It is a hash and not a version**: two builds of the same inputs produce the same value, nothing stores it, and it orders nothing.

generated_at.description: When Rail Center assembled this bundle. Informational — a reader caches on `content_hash`, never on this. `format` is an annotation in draft 2020-12 and most validators do not check it; nothing turns on this value here.

policies.description: The tenant's whole chain, unpaginated, and including disabled ones. Never truncated for length: a reader that received part of a chain would enforce part of a chain and have no way to tell.

bindings.description: Which policies reach which endpoint. A binding narrows. The key is always present, so a reader can tell "no endpoint is narrowed" from "this bundle does not describe bindings" without a special case.

enforcement.description: What Rail Center says to do with a call. Absent means a Rail Center older than RC-312, which a reader takes as judging nothing rather than as any posture in particular — inventing one enforces a decision the control plane never stated. Not in `required` for that reason.

mode.description: none — judge nothing, and keep polling so a move off it arrives. observe — evaluate, log every verdict, block none. enforce — evaluate, act, report denials. A component polls at all three: one that stopped at `none` could never be told it had been moved off it.

binding_fallback.description: What happens to a call no binding key matches at all. A property of the binding set, which is why it sits beside `bindings` rather than inside `enforcement` or inside a binding — a posture says how much of a verdict is acted on, this says what the verdict *is* where nothing matched, and it cannot live in a binding because it is precisely what applies when there is none. `block` refuses without consulting the chain; `pass` means *not refused for being unbound* and hands the call to the whole chain. Absent is `block`. Evaluated wherever the chain is walked and acted on only at `enforce`, so an operator sees what it would refuse before it refuses anything.

id.description: A UUID. Five spellings must parse — canonical, uppercase, braced, URN and undashed — and are compared in the canonical lowercase-hyphenated form. Rail Center emits the canonical one; the others arise in a bundle assembled elsewhere, and refusing them makes the bundle unusable, which refuses traffic.

name.description: What an operator reads. A policy with no readable name is named by its id rather than refused: no decision turns on it, and refusing the bundle would take enforcement down for a cosmetic fault.

condition.description: Left unconstrained on purpose. A condition that cannot be interpreted is refused *lazily*, where the walk reaches it, so that an earlier policy which already denied still gives that request a clean answer. Validating conditions here would make that refusal eager and change which requests get an answer.

action.description: What a match does. Any action other than `alert` denies. Unconstrained for the same reason as `condition`.

enabled.description: Skipped when exactly `false`, never merely falsy — the falsy sets do not agree across languages. A policy carrying no `enabled` key is enabled: a rule nobody switched off is one an operator expects to be running. Settled before anything else is validated, so that switching a policy off is a working remedy for a bundle this reader cannot parse. A policy carrying `enabled: false` is exempt from the priority rule in `allOf` below, because refusing a disabled policy's priority would refuse exactly the bundle that switching one off produces — which is the remedy this ordering exists to keep working.

priority.description: Ascending: 1 is evaluated before 2. A whole number within ±(2^53 − 1), because a priority arrives as a double and past that bound two values one reader sees as distinct another sees as a tie — and the chains then order differently. `1.0` is the integer 1; `1.5` is not a priority, and `true` is not one either.

endpoint_key.description: The endpoint this narrows — the *resolved* key, matched after any ingress rewrite, never the raw path. A rule written against a raw path is a rule a rewrite silently disarms. Must be a string: a language that coerces `123` narrows a request whose resolved key is the string "123".

mode.description: `gated` — only the policies in `policy_ids` apply. `open` — no policy applies to this endpoint, so nothing can deny and the request is allowed. Note *allowed*, not *skipped*: the bundle is still validated and the chain still ordered, because an unusable bundle is refused whatever any one endpoint's binding says. Anything else is refused, because the two guesses are "the listed policies apply" and "none do", which is the widest disagreement available.

policy_ids.description:
UUIDs naming policies in `policies`, in any of the five spellings, normalised before comparison — a raw comparison against a non-canonical id matches no policy, and an endpoint matching no policy is gated by nothing. Non-empty when `mode` is `gated`, empty when it is `open`; a gated entry naming nothing is refused, since "subject to nothing" is spelled `open` and "subject to everything" is spelled by carrying no entry.

An id naming no policy, or a disabled one, binds nothing and is not an error. A binding whose every id resolves to nothing leaves an empty chain, and an empty chain allows — do not fall back to the whole chain when narrowing empties it.
